title: The Eye as Microcosm: Visible and Hidden Likenesses, and the Mystery of Day-Sight
arc: The teaching opens by naming four types in the eye together with a fifth that is hidden, expands this to a cosmology of visible and hidden likenesses (fire, darkness, light, living air) interior to the human, and uses the riddle of why the pupil sees by day but not by night to disclose the descent of the First Man through the gate of the lower place into the four climes — Divine Truth coming forth and knowing every thing.
reading:
This chapter takes the human eye as a small living cosmos and reads from it the structure of the whole. The opening announces a count: there are four types — likenesses — that exist in the eye, and a fifth that is hidden within them. In correspondential terms, the eye is the understanding, the receptive faculty of light, and what is "in" the eye are the discrete degrees of receiving truth. The visible four answer to the natural-rational structure of seeing; the hidden fifth is the inmost mind that does not appear in the act of sight but is the source of seeing. The teaching is therefore working with the standard Manichaean figure of five-fold completeness, but split into a manifest set and a hidden one — the same pattern by which the Five Storehouses or the five faculties stand within the soul as a manifest fourfold ordered around an inmost unseen ground.

The text then widens the figure: there are four likenesses in human beings "who see while being seen," and within them four more that are hidden. This is the doctrine that every faculty of perception is itself perceived from above — the understanding looks outward and is at the same time looked through by what is interior to it. So a doubled fourfold appears: an outer ordered fullness (the senses and the apprehending mind in their visible operation) and an inner ordered fullness (the same faculties in their hidden, interior degree). Between these two ranks the elements are distributed: fire (love/will) is concealed in something — itself hidden to fire — and darkness belongs to death; over against this stands the Light who watches what is hidden in all things, and this watching Light is named the Living Air, the breath of perception by which the divine moves through every interior. The point is that in every act of seeing, fire and darkness lie concealed within, and what discriminates them is the Living Air — Divine Truth as living perception searching out what is hidden.

The hinge of the teaching is the riddle put plainly: why does the pupil of the eye habitually see by day but not, when night comes, do the same? Read correspondentially this is no question about ocular physics but about the conditions of spiritual sight. The pupil is the opening of the understanding, the gate of receptivity. It sees only when the Day shines — when a complete state of Light is present — and is shut up by Night, the state of falsity that covers truth. The teaching asks of what mystery this is the sign, and the answer it begins to unfold is cosmological: the pupil's day-sight signifies the gate of the lower place through which influx descends, the going-out and coming-in by which the upper place sends down its likenesses into the four climes, the ordered fullness of the natural extended in every direction. What the eye does in miniature, the cosmos does at large: a gate opens between an upper place and a lower place, and through that gate the divine descends into the fourfold of natural extension and remains there until the end.

The closing fragments draw this descent to a personal head. Something great is sent down, likened to what is above; the moment of the Living arrives; and the First Man comes forth from him and knows every thing. This is the consummating move: the four-and-fifth pattern in the eye, the visible-and-hidden likenesses in human beings, the gate between upper and lower, are all gathered into the single mission of Divine Truth descending into the natural. The First Man is the eye of the cosmos opened in the day of his coming. What was hidden — fire concealed within, darkness belonging to death, the inner four behind the outer four — becomes seen, because the Living Air (the Lord's perceiving Spirit) has gone out through the pupil-gate into all the climes. The teaching's spiritual argument is therefore this: the very structure of the eye is a witness that the understanding is regenerated only when Light from above descends through an opened gate; without that descent the inner fourfold is shut in night; with it, the First Man comes forth and there is nothing he does not know.

Because so much of the middle is in lacuna, the precise identification of the four visible and four hidden likenesses cannot be fixed; but the controlling figure — eye as gate, pupil as opening of the understanding, day-sight as influx of Divine Truth, night-blindness as the shutting of the gate, and First Man as the one who comes forth through the opened gate to know every thing — is stable across the surviving lines.
